{{short description|American botanist and author|bot=PearBOT 5}}
'''Peter Del Tredici''' is an American [[botanist]] and author. He is a former senior research scientist at [[Arnold Arboretum]] for 35 years and a [[Lecturer#United States|lecturer]] at the [[Harvard Graduate School of Design]]. He was appointed curator of the [[Larz Anderson Bonsai Collection]] in 1982 and was editor of the journal ''Arnoldia'' from 1989 to 1992.

Del Tredici, a native Californian, earned a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in [[Zoology]] from [[University of California, Berkeley]] in 1968 and a [[Master of Arts]] in [[Biology]] from the [[University of Oregon]] in 1969, after which he moved to Boston where he established his career and earned his [[Ph.D|doctorate]] in Biology from [[Boston University]] in 1991. His thesis adviser was [[Richard Primack]] and his thesis topic was "The Evolution and Natural History of Ginkgo biloba L.". Research on this project extended over a three-year period and involved travel to eastern China (fall of 1989) and to South Carolina.

{{Quote box
 |quote  = I consider 'weed' to be a politically incorrect term. There is no biological definition of the term weed. It's really a value judgment.
 |source = Peter Del Tredici<ref name=globe/>
 |width  = 50%
 |align  = right
}}
Del Tredici is an advocate of a "radically practical"<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.gardenrant.com/my_weblog/2010/10/peter-del-tredici.html |title=Peter Del Tredici gets real about 'wild urban plants' |author=Susan Harris |date=October 11, 2010 |work=Garden Rant |access-date=November 3, 2011}}</ref> approach to urban plant life, holding that what some people see as a collection of undesirable plants should be viewed as a valuable ecosystem unique to the hostile habitat of the city,<ref name=globe>{{cite web |url=http://archive.boston.com/bostonglobe/ideas/articles/2010/05/23/this_is_not_a_weed/ |title=This Is Not a Weed |author=Courtney Humphries |date=May 23, 2010 |work=Boston Globe |access-date=November 3, 2011}}</ref> and he prefers the term "spontaneous" over "invasive" in describing these flora.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2010/06/13/AR2010061304822.html |title=Harvard biologist comes to the defense of the much reviled tree of heaven |author=Adrian Higgins |date=June 14, 2010 |newspaper=Washington Post |access-date=November 3, 2011}}</ref> Del Tredici is the author of ''Wild Urban Plants of the Northeast: A Field Guide'', which catalogs and describes the many species of urban wildflowers, weeds, and other plants that flourish without human support, and in which he makes the case that they can be beneficial to the quality of urban life.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2010/09/16/AR2010091607742.html |title=Cultivating a meaningful reflection of yourself in the garden |author=Joel M. Lerner |date=September 18, 2010  |newspaper=Washington Post |access-date=November 3, 2011}}</ref>

Del Tredici also studied the ginkgo (''[[Ginkgo biloba]]'') for decades. He was part of a 1989 expedition that found wild ginkgos in [[Tianmu Mountain|Tian Mu Shan Reserve]], a notable find since this species had been long believed extinct in the wild.<ref name=harvard1>{{cite web |url=http://harvardmagazine.com/2011/11/the-living-dinosaur |title=The Living Dinosaur: Peter Del Tredici's search for the wild ginkgo |author=Jill Jonnes |date=November–December 2011 |work=Harvard Magazine |access-date=November 3, 2011}}</ref><ref>It is not undisputed that these are truly wild, as the population shows a relative genetic uniformity that could indicate that they were planted and preserved by Chinese monks over a long period (See {{cite journal |last1=Shen |first1=L |last2=Chen |first2=X–Y |last3=Zhang |first3=X |last4=Li |first4=Y–Y |last5=Fu |first5=C–X |last6=Qiu |first6=Y–X |title=Genetic variation of Ginkgo biloba L. (Ginkgoaceae) based on cpDNA PCR–RFLPs: inference of glacial refugia |journal=Heredity |volume=94 |issue=4 |pages=396–401 |year=2004 |pmid=15536482 |doi=10.1038/sj.hdy.6800616|doi-access=free }}), but later research by Wei Gong has indicated that the find likely was of wild trees.</ref> He demonstrated that ginkgo basal [[lignotubers]] develop from suppressed cotyledonary (embryonic leaf) buds – a [[resprouter|resprouting]] mechanism activated under stress that, according to Del Tredici, helps explain the ginkgo's long survival as a species. He helped develop supporting evidence for the theory that the ginkgo's characteristic vile–smelling fruits are a mechanism to attract ingestion by carnivores, aiding the tree's propagation via scat, and developed experiments confirming that all aspects of the ginkgo's sexual reproductive cycle are strongly influenced by temperature.<ref name="harvard1"/>

Del Tredici also consulted for a French subsidiary of [[Schwabe Pharmaceutical]] which markets ginkgo–leaf extract as a memory aid. While Del Tredici applied his expertise on the botanical side of the operation, he was skeptical that the products are effective, and noted that rather than deriving from ancient Chinese medical wisdom, the idea of ginkgo as an effective health agent "began in a board room in Germany in the mid–1960s" and has resulted in "a big cash cow".<ref>{{cite web |url=http://harvardmagazine.com/2011/10/ginkgo-and-memory |title=Ginkgo and Memory |author=Jill Jonnes |date=October 19, 2011 |work=Harvard Magazine |access-date=November 4, 2011}}</ref>

In 2013, Del Tredici was awarded a [[Veitch Memorial Medal]], given by the [[Royal Horticultural Society]] for outstanding contribution to the advancement of the science, art, or practice of horticulture.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://press.rhs.org.uk/Press-releases/2013-RHS-Awards-for-Outstanding-Contributions-to-H.aspx |title=2013 RHS Awards for Outstanding Contributions to Horticulture |date=April 11, 2013 |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society |access-date=December 15, 2014}}</ref>

==Publications==
Del Tredici has published scholarly articles in various journals, edited or co–edited books, and contributed sections to books.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://arboretum.harvard.edu/people/peter-del-tredici/ |title=Peter Del Tredici |publisher=Arnold Arboretum |access-date=November 3, 2011}}</ref> Works of which he is the author include:
